The video features a dissected brain in a laboratory setting with a person in a white lab coat explaining its anatomy. Initially, a gloved hand points with a metal tool at the thalamus and hypothalamus of the brain, highlighting the hypothalamic sulcus. Labeled text overlays appear: "Thalamus" (the thalamus is a sensory relay station), "Hypothalamus" (the hypothalamus controls body temperature, hunger, thirst, and hormone regulation), and "Hypothalamic Sulcus" (a groove separating the thalamus and hypothalamus). The woman in the white coat explains that the hypothalamus extends anteriorly to the anterior commissure and the optic chiasm, and inferiorly, it includes the mammillary bodies and extends to the infundibular stalk, where it communicates. After the dissection demonstration, the speaker, a woman wearing a white lab coat with black hair and a pearl necklace, turns towards the camera and begins to describe the brain. The background shows a sterile-looking room with green tiled walls and institutional settings.

The video begins with a close-up shot of a cross-section of a human brain mounted on a metal surface. A hand wearing a white surgical glove holds a surgical instrument and points to the fornix, a bundle of nerve fibers. The speaker then explains that the nerve fibers swing around the thalamus and descend to the columns of the fornix, just posterior to the anterior commissure. The speaker points out that the columns of the fornix project down to the mammillary bodies, and that the mammillothalamic tract connects the mammillary bodies with the anterior nucleus and the dorsal medial nucleus of the thalamus. The speaker points to the area she discusses using the surgical instrument. She says information from the thalamus travels to the limbic lobe. The video then transitions to a woman in a white lab coat with a black collared shirt. She has curly brown hair and is wearing a pearl necklace. She's in a room with neutral-colored walls, and a picture of a brain hangs on the wall behind her. She explains that this is the classic Papez circuit, involved in learning, memory, and emotion, but now they know that many other structures are involved in this circuit. The woman is speaking and gesturing directly to the camera with a slight smile. She breaks eye contact briefly, and then the video ends.

The video segment features an informative presentation about the anatomy of the brain. Initially, a cross-sectional view of a human brain is shown, along with a person in a white lab coat using a metallic pointer to specify the uncus, its hook-like appearance, as the anterior extension of the para-hippocampal gyrus, and the amygdala. Then the camera cuts to a medium shot of a woman, also wearing a white lab coat with “UBC Neuroanatomy” on its sleeve, explaining what is being shown, and then cuts back to a flat, top-down cross-section of a brain, again with a gloved hand using the pointer. The hippocampus is in the floor of the inferior horn and is distinguished by different layers of neurons giving it a striped appearance. When the cross-section is turned around, we are now more anterior and can see the amygdala, which is anterior and superior to the hippocampus. “Amygdala” is written in white text within a white outline, with a curved tail. The woman in the lab coat explains that the amygdala is key for emotion, memory, and basic drives. The camera cuts again to the woman in the lab coat, standing in front of a silver table on which there are several brain sections, and behind her, on the green wall, are three framed pictures showing various diagrams of the brain. Finally, the camera shows the woman in the lab coat pointing at a chalk drawing of the thalamus, hippocampus, fornix, mammillary body, amygdala, and lateral ventricle. The whole segment is informative, educational, and scientific in tone.
